newsitem.title: USA: US House passes bill extending CRP contracts.
newsitem.headline: US House passes bill extending CRP contracts.

text.p: The U.S. House, in a rebuke to Clinton administration dawdling, passed a bill Tuesday to allow farmers to unilaterally extend their Conservation Reserve contracts for one year.
The bill now goes to the Senate for consideration.
House Agriculture chairman Bob Smith, Oregon Republican, said the bill was "a one-time legislative remedy for a problem many of us have seen coming for months."
Smith and other farm-state lawmakers said they feared the Agriculture Department would wait too long to decide whether to accept bids to enroll land in the long-term reserve.
The bill was passed 325-92. A two-thirds vote was needed because the bill was debated under rules that barred amendments and curtailed debate.
Farmers could lose $600 million in fall-planted crops, chiefly winter wheat, if not given enough time to prepare fields and plant, according to Smith.
"Most of these farmers ought not, and will not, gamble on USDA making a decision," Smith said during floor debate.
Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman opposed the bill as needless, confusing and likely to keep productive land idle when the U.S. wheat stockpile needed to be replenished.
While backers said the bill would affect several million acres, Glickman said it might apply to 16 million acres, or half of the land now enrolled.
"If you want to do right for conservation programs and the environment, vote 'no' on this bill," Joe Skeen, chairman of the House Appropriations subcommittee, urged during debate.

Skeen, a New Mexico Republican, said the bill would block fragile land from entering the reserve but "it will allow farmers who have highly productive land the opportunity to collect a federal check for one more year."

Glickman said USDA was on track to notify farmers by late May if their land had been accepted, which he said was plenty of time. Skeptics were less certain the mammoth job would be done on time and pointed to how the department was months late in unveiling eligibility rules.
Contracts on 21 million acres in the reserve expire September 30. Farmers offered 25.6 million acres during a month-long sign-up during March.

Created in 1985, the Conservation Reserve pays farmers an annual rent to take fragile land out of production for 10 years. The goals of the reserve are to reduce erosion, protect water purity and provide wildlife habitat.
The Appropriations Committee has voted to limit new enrollments in the reserve to 14 million acres this year. A House vote on that bill was possible later in the week.
